description_full: DexCom, Inc., a medical device company, focuses on the design, development, and commercialization of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) systems for the management of diabetes and metabolic health in the United States and internationally. The company offers Dexcom G7 and G7 15 Day, an integrated continuous glucose monitoring system; Dexcom G6, a CGM system; Dexcom ONE+ to replace fingerstick blood glucose testing for diabetes treatment decisions; Stelo, a biosensor designed for adults with prediabetes and Type 2 diabetes who do not use insulin; Dexcom Share, a remote monitoring system; and Dexcom Follow application. It markets its products directly to endocrinologists, physicians, and diabetes educators. The company was incorporated in 1999 and is headquartered in San Diego, California.

financial_summary: DexCom, Inc. is a large-cap healthcare business with a $29.6B market cap on $4.7B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +17% over the past three years and +28% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +5.6pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 32% against a 10% cost of capital — a 21-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 64% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $1.1B in free cash flow — roughly 23 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.72× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -9.5% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 50× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.6%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
